title: Value vs Reference Types & ARC Memory
scopeHtml: Scope: struct vs class vs enum vs actor, copy-on-write, ARC, strong/weak/unowned, retain cycles, closures capture, deinit.

notes.title: Baseline and the memory model in one page
notes.html:
Android equivalent. On Android (ART/JVM) every object lives on a garbage-collected heap; you never free memory, but the GC may pause and a leaked reference keeps an object alive (the classic leaked Activity). In iOS there is no GC. Memory is managed by ARC (Automatic Reference Counting): the compiler inserts retain and release calls, and an object is destroyed deterministically the instant its count reaches zero.

Baseline. Swift 6 language mode, Xcode 16+, iOS 17/18 target. Concurrency-related capture rules (Sendable, actors) are mentioned here and developed in the concurrency notes.

 Kotlin / JVM                         Swift / ARC
 ------------                         -----------
 objects on GC heap                   struct/enum  -> inline (stack or inside owner)
 GC finds unreachable graph           class/actor  -> heap, refcount in object header
 pause, non-deterministic finalizer   deinit runs exactly when count hits 0
 cycles collected for free            cycles LEAK (you break them: weak/unowned)

The consequences are the whole topic: (1) types split into value (copied) and reference (shared) kinds, (2) cycles leak unless you break them, (3) deinit is predictable, so you can use it for cleanup and for leak detection.

Android iOS
data class struct (value type)
class class (reference type, ARC)
sealed class / enum enum (value type)
GC ARC
WeakReference<T> weak var
LeakCanary Memory Graph Debugger, Instruments Leaks, deinit prints
finalize() / Cleaner deinit (deterministic)

Everyday analogy. The JVM is a cleaning crew that walks the building at intervals and removes anything nobody is using. ARC is a "last one out turns off the lights" rule: each person holding the room counts; when the last person leaves, the lights go off immediately.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "Swift has a garbage collector" or "ARC is a GC". ARC is compile-time inserted counting; it cannot see cycles.
  • Believing leaks are impossible without manual memory management. Retain cycles are the iOS equivalent of leaked Activities.
  • Expecting deinit to be skipped "sometimes". It runs deterministically (but not at app termination).

notes.title: struct versus class versus enum versus actor
notes.html:
Android equivalent. In Kotlin nearly everything user-defined is a class on the heap (data class just adds generated methods). In Swift you choose among four nominal kinds, and structs and enums are the default; Apple's own guidance is "start with a struct".

Kind Semantics Stored Inheritance Identity Typical use
struct value, copied on assignment inline no (protocols only) no (== by value) models, view state, SwiftUI Views
enum value, one of N cases inline no no states, errors, results
class reference, shared heap + refcount single inheritance yes (===) shared mutable state, UIKit objects
actor reference, isolated heap + refcount none yes shared mutable state across threads
Languages: Swift · Kotlin
struct User: Equatable, Hashable, Codable {
    let id: Int
    var name: String
}
var a = User(id: 1, name: "Asha")
var b = a            // independent copy
b.name = "Ravi"
print(a.name)        // "Asha"
data class User(val id: Int, var name: String)
val a = User(1, "Asha")
val b = a.copy()     // you must ask for a copy
b.name = "Ravi"
println(a.name)      // "Asha"; plain assignment `val b = a` would SHARE the object

The crucial difference: in Kotlin val b = a shares the object, so mutating through b is visible via a. In Swift with a struct, var b = a makes a logically independent copy. That eliminates a whole category of "someone else mutated my object" bugs and makes structs trivially thread-safe to pass (they are Sendable when members are).

Choosing.

  • Use struct when the value is data, equality is by content, and no one needs a shared identity.
  • Use class when you need identity (a view controller, a file handle, a socket), inheritance from an Apple class (UIView, NSObject), shared mutable state, or deinit cleanup.
  • Use actor when the shared mutable state is touched from several threads/tasks.
  • Use enum when the value is exactly one of a closed set.

Mutation rules. A struct method that changes properties must be marked mutating; calling it requires a var. A let struct is deeply immutable. Classes have no such rule.

struct Counter {
    private(set) var value = 0
    mutating func increment() { value += 1 }
}
let c = Counter()
// c.increment()   // error: cannot use mutating member on immutable value 'c'

Equality. Structs get == free if you adopt Equatable and all members are Equatable (synthesised). Classes need a hand-written == or you compare identity with ===. Kotlin data class has generated equals/hashCode/copy/toString; Swift synthesises Equatable, Hashable, Codable on request but has no copy(...) (you mutate a copy).

Real industry examples. SwiftUI forces View to be a struct (cheap to recreate each render). Airbnb and Point-Free (Swift Composable Architecture) model app state as nested value types so that a reducer can compare "old state vs new state" and snapshot tests are trivial. UIKit classes (UIViewController) remain classes because they have identity and lifecycle.

Everyday analogy. A struct is a photocopy of a recipe card: you each scribble on your own copy. A class is the single shared whiteboard in the kitchen: everyone sees every change, and someone has to know when to erase it.

Common interview traps.

  • "Structs are always on the stack." Not guaranteed: a struct stored in a class, captured by an escaping closure, or inside an array lives in heap memory.
  • "Classes are slow." They cost an allocation and refcounting; structs holding references still pay ARC for those references.
  • Using class out of Java/Kotlin habit; reviewers will ask why it is not a struct.
  • Forgetting mutating and being confused by the compile error.

notes.title: Copy-on-write and how Array and String implement it
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Kotlin List copies are explicit (toMutableList() allocates a new array); val b = a shares. Swift Array, Dictionary, Set and String are structs with value semantics that stay cheap because they implement copy-on-write (COW).

Mechanism. Each collection struct holds a single reference to a heap buffer (a class instance with a refcount, capacity, count and elements). Assigning var b = a copies only that pointer and bumps the buffer's refcount: O(1). The first mutation through either variable checks isKnownUniquelyReferenced(&buffer); if the count is more than one, it allocates a new buffer, copies elements (O(n)), and mutates the copy.

var a = [1, 2, 3]       // buffer B1, refcount 1
var b = a               // b points to B1, refcount 2, no copy yet
b.append(4)             // refcount > 1 -> allocate B2, copy, then append; a still sees [1,2,3]
a.append(9)             // a is now unique owner of B1 -> mutate in place, no copy
 after `var b = a`            after `b.append(4)`
 a ---\                       a ---> [B1: 1,2,3]  rc=1
       > [B1: 1,2,3] rc=2     b ---> [B2: 1,2,3,4] rc=1
 b ---/

Building your own COW type. Standard library types do this internally; your own structs get it only if you implement it:

final class Storage { var items: [Int] = [] }

struct Bag {
    private var storage = Storage()
    var items: [Int] { storage.items }
    mutating func add(_ n: Int) {
        if !isKnownUniquelyReferenced(&storage) {      // shared? clone first
            let copy = Storage(); copy.items = storage.items; storage = copy
        }
        storage.items.append(n)
    }
}

String specifics. String is a 16-byte struct. Small strings (up to 15 UTF-8 bytes on 64-bit platforms; verify) are stored inline with no heap allocation and no refcounting. Larger strings use a heap buffer with COW semantics. Substring and ArraySlice share the parent's buffer, which is why holding a small substring can keep a huge parent buffer alive.

Performance traps.

  • Mutating a collection while another reference exists triggers a full copy: looping for i in 0..<n { copy = array; copy[i] += 1 } is O(n^2).
  • Passing an array to a function and the function mutating its local var copy triggers a copy; marking the parameter inout mutates the caller's buffer in place.
  • reserveCapacity(_) avoids repeated reallocation, like ArrayList(initialCapacity).
  • Arrays of classes copy the pointers only (plus retain each element), not the objects.
  • Large struct fields mean larger copies; keep structs small or wrap bulk data in an Array or a COW box.

Real industry examples. SwiftUI state (@State var items: [Item]) relies on COW to make "assign a new array to trigger re-render" cheap. Diffing libraries (DifferenceKit, CollectionDifference in the standard library) assume value semantics so snapshots of the old data are free.

Everyday analogy. Two people share one Google Doc link until one wants to edit; at that moment the editor gets a private duplicate. Anyone who is the only person with the link edits the original directly.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing assignment of an array copies all elements immediately. It copies lazily on first mutation.
  • Believing your custom struct is automatically COW. Only types wrapping a uniquely-checked buffer are.
  • Ignoring that COW makes thread safety non-trivial: the refcount check is atomic, but concurrent mutation of the same variable is still a data race.
  • Saying isKnownUniquelyReferenced works on a weak or unowned reference. It requires a strong class reference passed inout.

notes.title: ARC internals: retain, release and side tables
notes.html:
Android equivalent. The JVM stores a mark/age header in each object and a tracing GC discovers reachability. Swift stores a reference count in the object header and the compiler emits swift_retain / swift_release calls.

Object layout. A Swift class instance on a 64-bit platform begins with a 16-byte header: an 8-byte isa/metadata pointer (the type's metadata) and an 8-byte InlineRefCounts word. Properties follow. The refcount word packs: strong retain count (extra count beyond 1), unowned retain count, and flags (is deiniting, uses side table). Retain/release are atomic operations (hence a small cost on every reference copy, and why very hot loops over class references can show swift_retain/swift_release as top symbols in Time Profiler).

Side tables. When an object is referenced by a weak reference, or counts overflow the inline bits, the runtime allocates a side table that holds the strong, unowned and weak counts, and the object's refcount word then points to it. Weak references point at the side table (not at the object), which is how a weak reference can safely read "nil" after the object is destroyed: the side table outlives the object until the weak count reaches zero. This is why weak has slightly higher cost than strong, and why creating a weak reference to an object makes that object permanently use a side table (verify exact thresholds).

Count lifecycle.

 Foo()            strong=1 (the creator)
 let x = foo      strong=2  (copy of reference retains)
 x leaves scope   strong=1  (release)
 foo leaves scope strong=0  -> deinit runs, then memory is freed
                              (unowned count keeps the allocation until 0, weak side table until weak=0)

Compiler optimisation. The optimizer removes redundant retain/release pairs and, with OSSA (ownership SSA) improvements in recent compilers, more of them. You can influence it with borrowing, consuming parameter modifiers (Swift 5.9+), ~Copyable move-only types (Swift 5.9+, expanded in 6.0), and final classes (no dynamic dispatch). -Ounchecked, -O and whole-module optimisation affect results; always measure in a Release build.

func render(_ view: borrowing ViewModel) { }       // no retain needed for the call (verify copy rules)
struct FileDescriptor: ~Copyable {                  // move-only: no copies, deinit when consumed
    let fd: Int32
    deinit { close(fd) }
}

Real industry examples. Apple's performance docs and WWDC talks ("Understanding Swift performance", "Explore ownership control in Swift") show swift_retain/release overhead in hot paths. Teams at Uber and Lyft have published measurements of ARC cost when app startup does thousands of class allocations; the fix is usually to use structs, final, and lazy initialisation.

Everyday analogy. Each object has a small counter on its door: every person who takes a key adds a tally; each person leaving removes one. When the tally is zero the room is emptied at once. Weak watchers register at the front desk (the side table) so they can ask "is the room still there?" even after it is gone.

Common interview traps.

  • "ARC is free." Every reference copy is an atomic increment; in tight loops this matters.
  • Saying weak references point at the object. They point at the side table.
  • Saying deinit runs on a background thread always. It runs on whichever thread releases the last reference, which is why UI-touching deinit code can crash (see isolated deinit below).
  • Mixing up "ARC counts" and "reachability": an unreachable cycle still has positive counts, so it leaks.

notes.title: strong, weak and unowned
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Kotlin references are always strong; you use WeakReference<T> (and .get() null checks) to avoid leaks. Swift builds the three strengths into the language.

Keyword Counted? Optional? When the target dies Use for
(default) strong yes either keeps it alive owning relationships
weak no must be var, Optional becomes nil automatically delegates, parent back-pointers, closures that may outlive self
unowned no non-optional (or unowned(unsafe)) traps (crash) if accessed after death the other side is guaranteed to outlive you
Languages: Swift · Kotlin
final class Child {
    weak var parent: Parent?           // may become nil, so Optional var
}
final class Parent {
    var child: Child?
}
class Child { var parent: WeakReference<Parent>? = null }   // parent?.get() ?: ...
class Parent { var child: Child? = null }

unowned detail. An unowned reference does not retain but still counts toward the object's unowned count; the allocation is kept until that reaches zero, though deinit has already run. Accessing a dead unowned reference deterministically crashes with Fatal error: Attempted to read an unowned reference but object ... was already deallocated. That is a safe crash instead of silent memory corruption (unlike unowned(unsafe) or Objective-C unsafe_unretained, which can read freed memory).

Choosing weak vs unowned.

  • If the reference can legitimately be nil at some point: weak.
  • If lifetimes are strictly nested, like a credit card that cannot exist without its customer (unowned let customer: Customer): unowned.
  • When in doubt: weak. A nil is better than a crash in production.

Delegates. The standard iOS pattern uses weak var delegate: SomeDelegate? with a protocol constrained to classes (protocol SomeDelegate: AnyObject), exactly so that weak can be applied. UITableView.delegate and dataSource are weak for this reason.

protocol DownloadDelegate: AnyObject { func didFinish(_ data: Data) }
final class Downloader {
    weak var delegate: DownloadDelegate?
}

Real industry examples. UIKit delegates (UITableViewDelegate, URLSessionDelegate) are weak except URLSession's delegate, which the session retains strongly until invalidated, a famous memory trap: forgetting session.finishTasksAndInvalidate() leaks both session and delegate. Firebase and Alamofire hold their delegates weakly.

Everyday analogy. Strong is holding a balloon string: the balloon stays up while anyone holds one. Weak is pointing at the balloon: if all strings are let go it floats away and you see empty sky. Unowned is pointing at a balloon you swear is still there; if it is gone, you fall.

Common interview traps.

  • Declaring weak let (illegal) or weak on a non-class type.
  • Using unowned self in an async callback and getting crashes after the screen is dismissed.
  • Making delegate strong and creating a view-controller leak.
  • Thinking unowned references become nil. They don't; they trap.

notes.title: Retain cycles in closures and delegates
notes.html:
Android equivalent. On Android, a Handler/Runnable/anonymous listener holding an Activity leaks it until the message or listener is released; the GC handles pure cycles, so only "root-reachable" leaks matter. On iOS a pure cycle between two strong references is never collected.

Classic closure cycle.

final class ProfileViewModel {
    var onUpdate: (() -> Void)?
    var name = "A"

    func bind() {
        onUpdate = {                       // closure captures self strongly
            print(self.name)               // self -> onUpdate -> closure -> self  (cycle)
        }
    }
    deinit { print("VM freed") }           // never prints
}
 self --strong--> onUpdate (closure) --strong--> self      => refcount never 0

Fix by breaking one edge with a capture list:

onUpdate = { [weak self] in
    guard let self else { return }
    print(self.name)
}

Which closures actually cycle? Only closures stored by an object that the closure itself captures. A non-escaping closure (for example map, forEach, sorted) cannot cycle. DispatchQueue.main.async { self.x } does not cycle because the queue holds the closure only briefly; it extends self's lifetime until it runs, which is rarely a bug. Timer.scheduledTimer(withTimeInterval:repeats:block:) with a repeating timer that captures self does retain it until invalidate(), a very common leak.

Other cycle sources.

  • Two objects referencing each other strongly (parent <-> child) with no weak side.
  • Delegate declared strong.
  • NotificationCenter block-based observers (addObserver(forName:object:queue:using:)) keep the closure alive until removeObserver; capturing self strongly leaks. (Selector-based observers are auto-removed since iOS 9, block-based ones are not.)
  • CADisplayLink and Timer targets retain their target strongly.
  • Combine sink closures captured in self.cancellables (see below).
  • SwiftUI: an @Observable view model that stores a closure capturing a view's @State.

Real production incident pattern. A chat screen's view controller was never deallocated after dismissal; each visit added ~30 MB, producing Jetsam (out-of-memory kill) events visible in Xcode Organizer's Terminations report and MetricKit MXMetricPayload memory histograms. Root cause: a repeating Timer used for "typing" indicators captured self strongly. Fix: [weak self] plus timer.invalidate() in viewWillDisappear.

Everyday analogy. Two friends each insisting "I'll leave when you leave". Neither ever leaves, and the room (memory) is never freed. A weak reference is one friend who agrees to leave whenever the other does.

Common interview traps.

  • Adding [weak self] to every closure by reflex, including non-escaping ones and short-lived Tasks.
  • Believing DispatchQueue.async always causes a cycle.
  • Forgetting repeating Timer and NotificationCenter block observers.
  • Using [unowned self] when the closure can outlive self.

notes.title: weak self patterns, Task capture and Combine sinks
notes.html:
Android equivalent. In Kotlin you use viewModelScope.launch and the scope is cancelled for you; Flow collectors are tied to repeatOnLifecycle. In Swift you must reason about what holds the closure and what cancels it.

The guard-let-self pattern.

button.onTap = { [weak self] in
    guard let self else { return }      // Swift 5.7+ shorthand; strongifies for the closure body
    self.submit()
}

Inside the closure body, self is a temporary strong reference for the duration of one execution; that is safe and the idiom for UIKit callbacks. The older guard let strongSelf = self is the legacy spelling you meet in old code.

Task capture. A Task { } created inside a method captures self strongly for the lifetime of the task. That is not a permanent cycle unless the task itself is stored by self and never finishes or is not cancelled:

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
@MainActor
final class SearchViewModel {
    private var searchTask: Task<Void, Never>?
    var results: [String] = []

    func search(_ query: String) {
        searchTask?.cancel()                       // cancel the previous one
        searchTask = Task { [weak self] in         // avoids keeping VM alive if task hangs
            let items = (try? await API.search(query)) ?? []
            guard !Task.isCancelled, let self else { return }
            self.results = items
        }
    }
    deinit { searchTask?.cancel() }
}
class SearchViewModel : ViewModel() {
    private var job: Job? = null
    fun search(q: String) {
        job?.cancel()
        job = viewModelScope.launch {          // cancelled automatically in onCleared()
            results = runCatching { api.search(q) }.getOrDefault(emptyList())
        }
    }
}

Key difference: Task { } is unstructured and not tied to any scope. Nothing cancels it when the view model dies, so you cancel it yourself (in deinit, in SwiftUI with .task { } which cancels when the view disappears). SwiftUI's .task modifier is the preferred, auto-cancelled form. With a @MainActor class, Task { } inherits the actor isolation; Task.detached does not.

Combine sinks (legacy, you will meet it in old codebases).

import Combine
final class FeedViewModel {
    private var cancellables = Set<AnyCancellable>()
    @Published var items: [Item] = []

    init(service: FeedService) {
        service.itemsPublisher
            .receive(on: DispatchQueue.main)
            .sink { [weak self] items in self?.items = items }   // weak: self owns cancellables
            .store(in: &cancellables)
    }
}

Here self owns cancellables, which owns the subscription, which owns the closure: capturing self strongly closes a cycle. Using assign(to: \.items, on: self) also retains self strongly (a known pitfall; prefer assign(to: &$items) which does not retain, or sink with weak). In modern code, replace Combine with AsyncSequence/@Observable.

Real industry examples. Apple's Swift Evolution notes (SE-0365 allowing implicit self after [weak self] unwrap) formalised the guard pattern. Large apps such as Twitter/X's iOS client moved from RxSwift and Combine chains full of [weak self] to async/await to cut leak incidents.

Everyday analogy. A Task is a delivery driver you dispatch: unless you give them a recall number (cancel), they will keep driving to the house even if you moved. [weak self] is telling the driver "if nobody is home when you arrive, just go back".

Common interview traps.

  • Believing Task { self.x } always leaks. It holds self only until the task ends or is cancelled.
  • Forgetting to cancel stored tasks in deinit or onDisappear.
  • Using assign(to:on:self) in Combine and creating a cycle.
  • Assuming a Swift Task is cancelled automatically like viewModelScope.

notes.title: Detecting leaks with Memory Graph Debugger and Instruments
notes.html:
Android equivalent. LeakCanary and Android Studio's heap dump/Memory Profiler. iOS has equivalents built into Xcode.

Cheapest check: deinit logging. In debug builds, print inside deinit. If it never prints after dismissing a screen, you have a leak. Combine with an assertion helper in tests (weak var ref, release the owner, #expect(ref == nil)).

@Test func viewModelDeallocates() async {
    weak var weakVM: ProfileViewModel?
    do {
        let vm = ProfileViewModel()
        weakVM = vm
        vm.bind()
    }
    #expect(weakVM == nil)       // fails if a retain cycle exists
}

Debug Memory Graph (Xcode). Run the app, press the Debug Memory Graph button (three connected circles) in the debug bar. Xcode pauses the process, lists every live object, and flags leaked instances with purple exclamation marks. Selecting an object shows the strong reference graph; a cycle shows as a loop. Turn on Malloc Stacks (Live Allocations Only) in the scheme's Diagnostics so each object shows the allocation backtrace. Use the filter "Show only leaked blocks".

Instruments.

  • Leaks template: finds unreachable allocations (it cannot see leaks that are still reachable, such as a leaked-but-referenced view controller).
  • Allocations: track "Persistent" bytes per class; use Mark Generation (Generation Analysis) before and after a navigation round trip to see which classes grew. A view controller class still present after pop proves a retain issue even when Leaks shows nothing.
  • VM Tracker, Time Profiler (to spot retain/release hot spots).

Production monitoring. Xcode Organizer shows memory and termination metrics (including "Terminated due to memory" and Jetsam). MetricKit's MXMetricPayload delivers memory peak and average; Sentry, Firebase Crashlytics and Datadog capture OOM events (iOS does not deliver a crash for Jetsam, so SDKs infer it from the next launch state; verify).

Zombies. The Zombie Objects diagnostic (scheme > Diagnostics) keeps deallocated objects as zombies and logs the message sent to a freed object. It detects use-after-free in Objective-C/unsafe paths; it does not find leaks and increases memory use, so debug only.

Address/Thread Sanitizer and static tools. Address Sanitizer catches use-after-free and buffer overruns in unsafe code. Thread Sanitizer catches data races (essential with Swift 6). SwiftLint plus custom rules and the -warn-concurrency/strict concurrency flags catch capture issues earlier.

Real industry examples. Meta's FBRetainCycleDetector (Objective-C) popularised automated cycle detection; many teams embed a MLeaksFinder-style check in debug builds that asserts that a popped view controller deallocates within seconds.

Everyday analogy. A leak hunt is a plumber with a dye test: run water (navigate and dismiss), mark the generation, then see which pipes still hold coloured water.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying Instruments Leaks finds all memory problems. Retained-but-reachable growth (abandoned memory) is invisible to Leaks and needs Allocations generations.
  • Profiling a Debug build; ARC optimisations differ in Release.
  • Forgetting that a leak graph only shows after interacting with the screen, not at idle.
  • Relying on Zombies to find retain cycles.

notes.title: deinit and isolated deinit
notes.html:
Android equivalent. finalize() is non-deterministic and discouraged; you clean up in onDestroy, onCleared, close(). Swift's deinit runs exactly when the strong count hits zero, synchronously, on the releasing thread.

final class FileLogger {
    private let handle: FileHandle
    init(url: URL) throws { handle = try FileHandle(forWritingTo: url) }
    deinit { try? handle.close() }          // deterministic cleanup (RAII)
}

Rules.

  • No parameters, no explicit call; superclass deinit runs automatically after the subclass's.
  • Do not resurrect self (store it elsewhere) in deinit.
  • Do not start long operations or await in deinit (it is synchronous and not async).
  • Structs and enums have no deinit (non-copyable ~Copyable types do, since Swift 5.9).
  • Not called at normal app termination or on exit(), so don't rely on it for flushing critical data.

The isolation problem. In Swift 6 a @MainActor class's deinit is nonisolated: it can run on any thread, because the last release may happen anywhere. So deinit cannot freely touch @MainActor properties. Before Swift 6.1 you worked around it with MainActor.assumeIsolated (wrong if called off-main) or by moving cleanup to an explicit invalidate() method.

Isolated deinit (SE-0371, Swift 6.1 / Xcode 16.3+ ; verify availability and deployment-target back-deployment) lets you write:

@MainActor
final class MapController {
    var observers: [NSObjectProtocol] = []
    isolated deinit {                      // runs on the main actor
        observers.forEach(NotificationCenter.default.removeObserver)
    }
}

The runtime hops to the actor to run the deinit body if needed, so the object lives slightly longer than the release. For actor classes the same applies. Until you can use it, keep non-isolated deinit limited to Sendable resource cleanup.

Production incident patterns.

  • deinit of a view controller releasing the last reference to a big image cache on the main thread, causing a main-thread hang visible in Organizer's Hang rate (stall) metrics.
  • A watchdog kill (0x8badf00d) when deinit of a singleton-owned object synchronously closes a database during suspend. Move to applicationDidEnterBackground cleanup.
  • Crash when a deinit accesses a @MainActor view from a background thread (main-thread checker or Swift 6 isolation runtime check).

Real industry examples. RAII-style deinit is used in Realm (closing handles), Core Data wrappers and NSKeyValueObservation tokens (invalidated when the token deallocates, so storing it keeps the observation alive).

Everyday analogy. deinit is the closing-time checklist that runs the moment the last staff member leaves; if the last person out is not the manager (main actor), they may not be authorised to lock certain doors, which is the isolation issue.

Common interview traps.

  • Expecting deinit on the main thread. It runs where the last release happens.
  • Putting await or Task that captures self inside deinit; self is already dying.
  • Relying on deinit to save user data on app exit.
  • Asserting "VM is deinitialised" in a test while a stored Task still holds self.

notes.title: Memory layout: stack, heap and existential containers
notes.html:
Android equivalent. On the JVM primitives live on the stack/inline, objects on the heap, with boxed Integer for generics. Swift lets you inspect sizes with MemoryLayout.

MemoryLayout<Int>.size           // 8
MemoryLayout<Bool>.size          // 1
MemoryLayout<Int?>.size          // 9 (value + 1 tag byte), stride 16
struct S { var a: Bool; var b: Int; var c: Bool }
MemoryLayout<S>.size, MemoryLayout<S>.stride, MemoryLayout<S>.alignment   // 17, 24, 8

size vs stride vs alignment. size is bytes of payload; stride is the distance between consecutive elements in an array (size rounded up to alignment); alignment is the address multiple. Reordering fields (a: Bool, c: Bool, b: Int) reduces size to 10 and stride to 16: a real optimisation for large arrays of structs. Swift does not reorder stored properties for you (verify; the compiler keeps declaration order for ABI-stable types).

Stack vs heap. A local struct or enum value usually lives in the stack frame or registers. It moves to the heap when it is a stored property of a class, is captured by an escaping closure (the closure context box is heap-allocated), is stored in a collection's buffer, or when it is too large or its size is not known at compile time. final class instances can sometimes be stack-promoted by the optimizer when proven not to escape. Heap allocations cost malloc plus refcounting plus cache misses; Instruments' Allocations shows them, and Time Profiler shows swift_allocObject/swift_release in hot paths.

Existential containers (any Protocol). A value of protocol type is stored in a fixed-size existential container of 40 bytes on 64-bit: a 3-word inline value buffer (24 bytes), a pointer to the type's metadata, and a pointer to the protocol witness table (method table). If the concrete type fits in 3 words it is stored inline; larger values are heap-allocated and the buffer holds a pointer (with COW semantics). Calls go through the witness table (dynamic dispatch). A generic function func f<T: P>(_ t: T) is specialised by the compiler to concrete code with no container (static dispatch, inlinable), and some P also keeps the concrete type (see 03_L3).

 any Drawable (existential container, 40 bytes on arm64)
 +-----------+-----------+-----------+-----------------+-------------------+
 | word 0    | word 1    | word 2    | type metadata * | witness table *   |
 | inline value buffer (24 bytes)    |                 |                   |
 +-----------+-----------+-----------+-----------------+-------------------+
   value > 24 bytes => buffer holds pointer to heap box

Class instance layout. 16-byte header (metadata pointer plus refcounts) then properties; dispatch through the class vtable unless final/private; @objc dynamic uses Objective-C message sending (needed for KVO, selectors). Keep classes final by default for speed and clarity.

Enum layout. Payload enums use the max payload size plus a tag (bits may be borrowed from spare bits). indirect enum boxes payloads on the heap (recursive types).

Real industry examples. WWDC "Understanding Swift Performance" (2016) is the canonical reference for the existential container and witness table; Apple's own SwiftUI uses some View to avoid existential overhead and enable diffing of concrete types.

Everyday analogy. The existential container is a standard shipping crate of fixed size: small items fit inside, big items sit in a warehouse with a note in the crate pointing to them; every crate has a label (metadata) and a manual (witness table) taped on.

Common interview traps.

  • Using size to compute array memory; it is stride that matters.
  • Saying "protocol-typed values are slow because they are on the heap". Small ones are inline; the cost is dynamic dispatch plus 40 bytes plus possible boxing.
  • Believing a struct never touches the heap.
  • Quoting layout numbers as guarantees; they are implementation details except for ABI-stable system types (verify).

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• iOS uses ARC, not a GC: deterministic destruction, but cycles leak and you break them.
  • Default to struct and enum; use class for identity, inheritance or shared state, actor for isolated shared state. Swift has no copy() on structs; assignment copies.
  • Collections and strings are structs with copy-on-write over a uniquely-checked heap buffer; slices and substrings retain their parent.
  • Objects carry a header with a refcount; weak references use a side table; every retain/release is an atomic cost.
  • weak becomes nil, unowned traps, delegates are weak and class-constrained.
  • Closure cycles arise only when a stored closure captures its owner; repeating Timers, block observers and Combine sinks are the common leaks.
  • Task { } is unstructured; cancel it yourself or use SwiftUI .task.
  • Find leaks with deinit logging, tests with weak references, Debug Memory Graph, and Instruments Allocations generations; monitor Jetsam with Organizer and MetricKit.
  • deinit is synchronous on the releasing thread; isolated deinit (Swift 6.1, verify) addresses actor-isolated cleanup.
  • any Protocol values live in a 40-byte existential container; generics and some avoid it.
